clue.text: Good scope offered by initial moves

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
an ambit is the scope or extent of something

explanation.surface: Someone praises the wide options opened up by the first moves in a game of chess.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess setting makes 'Good scope' read as praise, but it splits into the abbreviation and a word for extent.
explanation.definitionFit: A chess gambit is an opening sequence in which a player sacrifices material early for position, a planned set of opening plays.

clue.text: Quick taking a short breather before start of event

indicators.note: something cut short is missing its end, so the last letter is dropped
the start of a word is where it begins, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a fish breathes through its gills, so a gill is a breathing organ
the opening letter of event

explanation.surface: A sprinter, nimble on their feet, takes a brief rest just before the race begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breather' suggests a short rest, but it is the organ a fish breathes with; trimmed to GIL, it follows the A and precedes E.
explanation.definitionFit: Agile describes someone able to move fast and easily, nimble and lively, a straightforward synonym for quick.

clue.text: Ashamed to make money working in sport

blocks.note: to feel bad about something is to be ashamed of it
to mint is to make coins
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: An athlete feels guilty about turning professional and earning a living from their sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' is usually an anagram signal, but here it simply gives ON, as in a switched-on machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is a racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net, one example of a sport.

clue.text: Rant made by one in commerce

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
commerce is buying and selling, trade

explanation.surface: A businessperson goes off on an angry rant about the state of commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: Putting the numeral inside the word for commerce after its first letter gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of criticism, exactly the kind of outburst called a rant.

clue.text: Money gets plain wool

blocks.note: cash is money
mere means plain or simple, as in 'a mere child'

explanation.surface: Having money only buys you ordinary, plain wool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like it describes the wool, but it is the adjective MERE, as in nothing more than.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is the fine soft fibre from Kashmir goats, a luxury kind of wool used for knitwear.

clue.text: Company calls about poor lads working in US city

indicators.note: letters that are working are busy moving about, so they get rearranged
to go about something is to go around it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
to ring someone is to call them on the phone
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A firm phones round about some impoverished young men with jobs in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calls about' means the calls go around the jumbled lads, with the company attached at the front of the shell.
explanation.definitionFit: Colorado Springs is a large city in the state of Colorado, at the foot of Pikes Peak.

clue.text: Horse-drawn carriage, second phaeton, abandoned

indicators.note: behaving with abandon means wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
taken as written

explanation.surface: A list entry: a horse-drawn carriage, a second-hand phaeton, left behind somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A phaeton is itself a horse-drawn carriage, which makes it look like the definition; it is only letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanhope is a light open one-seater carriage with two or four wheels, named after the clergyman who first had one built.

clue.text: Worth millions, flag that's turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up flips it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for million(s)
to flag is to tire, grow weary

explanation.surface: A banner that has been hoisted up is said to be worth a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' pretends to be a banner, but it is the verb meaning to weaken or grow weary.
explanation.definitionFit: Merit is value or excellence that deserves reward, the same idea as someone's or something's worth.

clue.text: Unprincipled person could bring about authentication of a will

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
probate is the legal proving of a will

explanation.surface: A scoundrel might set about getting a will legally proved so as to inherit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring about' reads as one phrase meaning cause, but 'about' belongs to the wordplay on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is someone of immoral, unscrupulous character, a rogue with no principles.

clue.text: Show wine store for the most part stocking popular red knocked back

indicators.note: most but not all of something is used, so the final letter goes
something knocked back is sent backwards, so it reads the other way
a shop stocking goods holds them inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: wine is kept in a cellar
what is in is popular
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine merchant mostly keeps popular red wine that gets drunk quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests downing a drink, but it turns the colour round. A pantomime is a British family Christmas stage show, and this is one of the best-known.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinderella is a fairy tale regularly staged as a Christmas pantomime, so it is a theatrical production.

clue.text: Ready to complain if starter's not included

indicators.note: a starter is the first course, and leaving it out drops the opening letter

blocks.note: to gripe is to complain

explanation.surface: A diner is set to grumble if the meal comes without a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' reads as a restaurant first course, but it is the first letter of the word for complain.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that is ripe is fully developed and fit to eat, and a plan ripe for action is prepared.

clue.text: Confuse playwright in Berlin? Not half!

indicators.note: not half keeps only half the word, so the second half is thrown away
one thing sitting in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright
the city name, taken as written before it is halved

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an English-language dramatist in Berlin would be confused, and gets the emphatic reply 'Not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely', but here it literally keeps half of the city's name, and the dramatist goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewilder someone is to perplex them thoroughly, leaving them puzzled and unable to understand.

clue.text: Illegally obtained pet food?

blocks.note: stolen goods are called hot
a dog is a typical pet

explanation.surface: It asks whether stolen pet food is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that read literally the answer is a stolen dog, not a snack.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot dog is a sausage served in a split bread roll, a familiar kind of fast food.

clue.text: Previous over

blocks.note: first meaning: former, earlier
second meaning: finished and gone, as in the danger is over

explanation.walkthrough: Two plain words, each a meaning of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both earlier in time, as an adjective, and finished, as when a crisis is described as done.

clue.text: Disparaging remark when being taken round island

indicators.note: something taken round another encircles it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a being is a person
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Someone makes a snide comment while being given a tour of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a verb in 'being taken round', but it is a noun for a creature or person.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast aspersions is to make damaging, belittling comments about someone's character or reputation.

clue.text: Envoy's academic qualification, first from Trinity

indicators.note: the first taken from a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: a diploma is a certificate of academic achievement
the opening letter of Trinity

explanation.surface: An ambassador's degree was the first one awarded by Trinity College.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay rather than showing possession.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy is a messenger or representative sent on a mission abroad by a government, a kind of ambassador.

clue.text: Old poet wrong over colour

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips it so it reads upward

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a bard is a poet
evil is wrongdoing

explanation.surface: An ageing poet has fallen out with someone about a choice of colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet and the wrong are reversed together as one string, so their order swaps as well as their letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive drab is the dull greyish-green shade used for military uniforms, one particular hue.

clue.text: Page carried on, took it as read

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for page
to resume is to carry on after a pause

explanation.surface: A reader turned the page and kept going, assuming they had understood it.
explanation.walkthrough: The reading picture makes 'took it as read' sound literal, but it is the idiom for assuming.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something as read is an idiom for assuming it is true without checking, which is what presuming means.

clue.text: Indignant, well-informed elected members

blocks.note: to be up on a subject is to be well-informed about it
a candidate who is elected is in
arms are limbs, which are members of the body

explanation.surface: Knowledgeable members of parliament are outraged about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elected members' suggests politicians, but members here are limbs of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: To be up in arms is an idiom for being angry and protesting loudly, which is to be indignant.

clue.text: Almost perfect plan

indicators.note: almost is not quite all, so the final letter is left off

blocks.note: ideal means perfect

explanation.surface: A scheme that is nearly flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost perfect' reads as praise for the plan, but it trims a synonym of perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea can be a proposed scheme or intention, as in 'my idea is to leave early', so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Pressure applied to speak in golf club

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure
to utter is to speak

explanation.surface: A golfer feels the pressure when asked to speak at the club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf club' reads as the venue for a speech, but it is the implement.
explanation.definitionFit: A putter is the flat-faced club a golfer uses on the green to roll the ball towards the hole.

clue.text: Credit is doubled in emergency

blocks.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
the word is written twice

explanation.surface: Borrowing twice as much when money is tight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubled' sounds financial next to credit, but it just means the little word appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a time of acute danger or difficulty needing urgent action, the same as an emergency.

clue.text: Note coming from small plucked instrument

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
the harp is played by plucking its strings

explanation.surface: A musical note is produced by a little stringed instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about music, so the definition hides in plain sight among the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp is a note raised by a semitone, such as F sharp, so it names a musical pitch.

clue.text: Way to secure permit for gambling game

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: a route is a way
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: Someone seeks a method of obtaining a licence to run gambling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Permit' looks like a noun meaning licence, but it is the verb, giving a short synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Roulette is the casino game where players bet on which numbered pocket a ball lands in on a spinning wheel.

clue.text: A test in translation may give one experience

indicators.note: translation turns words into another form, so the letters are rendered in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Sitting a translation exam might give a student some useful practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Experience' is a noun here, as in a taste of freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste of something is a brief first-hand encounter with it, such as a taste of success.

clue.text: Prima donna very keen to return

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: avid means very keen

explanation.surface: An opera star is eager to come back for another season.
explanation.walkthrough: The comeback picture hides the instruction to read the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A prima donna is the leading female opera singer, and diva is the other name for such a star.

clue.text: One into finance is enthralled by French painter and what he produced

indicators.note: someone enthralled is captivated, held inside another's spell

blocks.note: Claude Monet, the French Impressionist
a painter produces art
taken as written

explanation.surface: A financier is captivated by an Impressionist and his paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One into finance' sounds like any money enthusiast, but it defines a follower of an economic doctrine.
explanation.definitionFit: A monetarist believes the economy is best managed by controlling the money supply, a school of thought in economics.

clue.text: Decidedly trendy black suit

blocks.note: what is in is fashionable
spades is one of the two black suits in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A fashionable black suit is emphatically in style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' suggests clothing, but it is a suit of playing cards.
explanation.definitionFit: In spades is an idiom meaning to a great degree, emphatically, much like an adverb of certainty.

clue.text: In centre of Perth, mate there caught out thief

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter
a letter brought in takes the place of another
a letter sent out makes room for its replacement

blocks.note: the middle letter of Perth
cobber is Australian slang for a mate, and Perth is in Australia
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: In the middle of Perth, an Australian's friend was caught and the thief escaped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' refers back to Perth, so the mate is an Australian one; the Perth letter replaces the caught letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber is someone who steals, especially by force or threat, so the word is a synonym for thief.
